title: Why the minority is kept (Mishnah Eduyot 1:5)
hookLine: minority opinions are recorded so a later court might rely on them
last: MIDRASH LISTENS TO THE TORAH'S SILENCES.

cards: A vote is taken. The motion passes. The sensible next step is to write down the result and move on; in a year, nobody remembers what the no side argued.
The Mishnah does something stranger. Page after page, it records the ruling and also the name of the person who disagreed, what he said, and sometimes why. Why keep a losing argument at all?
In tractate Eduyot, the Mishnah stops to answer that very question about itself.

teach.b: Why the minority is kept. It's the Mishnah's own explanation, in Eduyot, of why it records a single opinion that lost. First, the question as it asks it.
The law follows the majority. So why mention the words of one person against the many?

teach.h: A LATER COURT MIGHT RELY ON IT.
teach.b: Second, its answer: so that if a later court sees that lone opinion and agrees with it, that court can rely on it.
The minority view is kept on the shelf, not thrown away, with a name attached, for a different time that might need it. Third, the fine print.

teach.h: GREATER IN WISDOM AND IN NUMBER.
teach.b: The Mishnah adds that a court can't overturn the ruling of an earlier court unless it is greater than it, in wisdom and in number. That's a high bar.

Some commentators put the two halves together: the minority view was part of the original discussion, so a later court can lean on it without having to overturn anyone. On that reading, the door was left open on purpose.
Fourth, another voice, right next to it.

The very next mishnah gives Rabbi Yehudah's reason, and it's different: the minority view is recorded so that if someone says, I have a tradition that says this, others can answer: you heard the opinion of that one sage, and the law didn't follow him.
One reason keeps the view alive; the other keeps it labeled.
And the Mishnah, true to form, keeps both reasons.

how: Students of Mishnah and Talmud learn the minority opinions alongside the rulings, and later legal authorities sometimes cite a minority view when a situation calls for it.

games.q: what does “why the minority is kept” mean?
o: so a later court might rely on the losing view
so the losing sage is honored for his effort
so readers can see just how close a vote was

games.q: why the minority is kept — tap the pairs.
p: a later court might rely on it
so it's known as the minority view
greater in wisdom and in number

s: the Mishnah records only the winning rulings
it records the lone opinions too, with names, and explains why in Eduyot.
a later court can rely on a recorded minority view
that is the Mishnah's first reason for keeping it.
the Mishnah gives only one reason for keeping the minority
the next mishnah adds Rabbi Yehudah's reason: so the view is known as the minority's.

games.q: you're editing the Mishnah. the law follows the majority, and one sage disagreed. what do you do with his words?
o: cut them; the law is settled.
keep them, with his name, in case a later court needs them.
rewrite them so he seems to agree.
games.why: Eduyot keeps them, so a later court might rely on them, and, in Rabbi Yehudah's reason, so they stay labeled as the minority.

practice: Bring to mind an opinion you don't hold, and find its strongest version, the one its best defender would sign, not a straw one.

If you have a pen or your phone, write it in one sentence, with a name beside it if it belongs to someone. Then hold it carefully for a moment, labeled, the way the Mishnah shelves a view in case one day it's needed.

wordCard.voice: Why the minority is kept. The Mishnah's reason for recording losing opinions: a later court might rely on them, and they stay labeled as the minority. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: an individual. The Mishnah contrasts the words of the yachid with those of the many.

carryVoice: Your line: the minority is kept. The losing side might be needed, and it should be known for what it is. Until tomorrow.
